title: BREAKING: Lummis UNVEILS new crypto bill, BLASTS the ‘BANKERS’
transcript_text: Welcome back. Good Thursday morning, everybody. Thanks so much for joining us this morning. I'm Maria Bartre-Romo and it is Thursday, July 23rd. I hope you have a great Thursday morning. It is almost 7 a.m. on the button on the East Coast. The Senate releasing the long awaited updated text for the landmark crypto regulatory bill. That is the Clarity Act. The House passed it over a year ago. But the Senate has been working to get its version of the legislation ready for months now. We are about to talk with Cynthia Lumis, who is the senator, overseeing this process and has delivered as she promised. Shope Sony, this is important as the U.S. strives to be number one in digital assets going forward across the world. And to have that regulatory framework so that the market, investors, companies, individuals can move forward. And it's time to move forward. And you want this regulatory framework in place and that's what Clarity delivers. And you know, without Clarity, you don't really have genius. You know, those two pieces of legislation really go hand in hand. I mean, I think that, and I have to applaud Senator Tim Scott, his leadership on Clarity has been nothing short of incredible. And the understanding seems to be there among many of the senators that have joined you on this program, that it is time to get this to the finish line. Understand, though, when I understand as do you, though, that the banks had their concerns and you've spoken with Jamie Diamond about those concerns, that, you know, you don't want to give basically all these benefits and perks to these companies with, and then not have them under the same regulatory framework as a bank, understood. And that's the crux of the issue, which you reported unconsensibly, yeah. I mean, that was largely the crux at one point, but I think the issues for Democrats have moved now to ethics issues. And Jonathan, one of the issues is that the Democrats are trying to put language in this bill that will preclude President Trump and his family from making any money in crypto. And I'm going to tell you, if this language is aggressive in terms of not allowing the President and others, his family, friends, whatever, to actually engage in crypto business, the President's just going to veto it. Jonathan? Yeah, it just shows really where the Democrats are because everything they do is about trying to harm President Trump, trying to make him look bad as opposed to what's good for the American people. That's what the issue should be. And President Trump wants to be a leader in crypto, a leader in AI, and instead of joining him on these issues, which are totally common sense, they'd rather use it as an opportunity to take a pot shot at him, his family, to try to harm them. And you're right, he will veto it because it's not only unnecessary, it's nonsense and a distraction. Yeah, and we'll see. We're going to talk with Cynthia Lama shortly to find out specifically what the language says and how it has changed. And if she expects that she will get support, even from Democrats, for this bill. But you're right, Cheryl. The other issue is the idea that crypto platforms would be able to pay rewards to customers who put stablecoins in their platform, the crypto platform, and the banks are worried that they're going to, that's going to mean that they're going to take money out of traditional deposit accounts. We haven't seen any evidence of that. The people are taking money out of deposit accounts, by the way. In fact, the last couple of banks that we reported on, which are on earnings last week, their deposits were up. So join me right now, and if Fox Business Exclusive is Wyoming Senator Cynthia Lama. Senator, great to have you this morning. Thank you so much for being here. My pleasure, Maria, thanks for having me. And thanks for your leadership on this bill. You are the chairwoman of the Senate Subcommittee on Digital Assets. Can you tell us more about this updated language and what your expectations are for the clarity act? Maria, we put out language with the comprehensive bill yesterday. So people could see what it looks like to have the agriculture's work, the banking committees work, the ethics committees work, the judiciary's committees work, all combined into one piece of legislation. And yes, we're still challenged by the bankers allegations that this will reduce deposit assets and make less money available for lending. There's actually no proof of that, as you just pointed out, deposits and banks are up since the Genius Act passed a year ago, and yet that is what they're trying to amend. They're trying to use the clarity act to amend the Genius Act that passed a year ago, even though there's no indication that it's going to hurt their deposit. So we're fighting against and trying to work against something, there's no proof of. It's just a concern. We're also dealing, of course, with the president's willingness to subject himself and Melania Trump to the most restrictive ethics language that a president has ever subjected himself to. But of course, there's no policing Democrats at this point. So we're facing some headwinds. Yeah, I know that. And let me get your take on that, because it seems like you're going to have to even make more concessions on the language around ethics to secure the Democrats' support, right? Because look, you had several Democrats, yet last night, voicing concerns about the updated tax, particularly around the bill's enforcement mechanism. That place's responsibility on the Attorney General, is that the issue right now? That is kind of a bright line. We had worked until there was an impact with Democrats earlier this month, because they want state attorneys general to be able to sue elected officials that are subject to this ethics law. And so that would allow, for example, an attorney general from another state to sue me if they thought I violated the ethics law. So when I ran that by senators, they said, we don't want that. And so this ethics provision is not just applicable to the president and the vice president. It's applicable to every House member, every senator, and every federal judge. So we're trying to not plan legislation around one person who holds one office for the next two years, but rather over time that will serve the House, the Senate, the judiciary, and the executive branch in a fair way. The struggle is, of course, a lot of Democrats are absolutely focused on one person. And that's President Trump. So since President Trump actually agreed that he would have the choice to either put his assets in a blind trust or divest of his participation in digital assets and companies that derive revenue from digital assets, somehow that's not enough. I think it's going to be a struggle. Fortunately, Tom Tellus is working with Democrats to continue to try to find a way that they could support the ethics provisions in this bill. But it's hard for me to see it right now because they're so focused on getting a pound of flesh from President Trump. I mean, do you think, so you do think that the president will accept some guardrails here. I mean, you think that the president will accept some provisions, but it's not going to be enough for the Democrats. I mean, they want to get this passed. They understand the need to be number one across the world in digital assets, though, right? Well, I hope so. And quite frankly, what, 90 percent of the spot market is overseas, 80 percent of the digital asset futures market is overseas, I don't know if they understand how significant it would be if the Clarity Act failed. And we allowed this industry to continue to grow and mature overseas because they won't come back once they get certainty in Singapore, for example. They'll stay there. So it's important that we address this now. I do believe that we'll continue to work on it for the next few days. But we've been working on it for 11 months, and maybe the last six of those months have been seven days a week. So there's a point at which we just have to vote, Maria. We just have to vote. Yeah, you've done such a great job on this, Senator. And so what are you looking at? You're looking at like eight or ten Democrat votes that you need to actually end debate and get this across the finish line. Or do you expect that even if you get that, that the president could still veto it? The president won't veto the ethics language that is in there now. And I don't see any other substantive provisions of the bill preventing the president from signing the bill. So the problem is not the president. The problem seems to lie in the U.S. Senate. The banks are putting on a full court press that's scaring some senators. The ethics part with the Democrats is still a sticking point, I believe. So next week, we've got Lindsey Graham Memorial Service on Tuesday, Lindsey Graham Funeral on Wednesday. So we'll have some absenteeism. Quite frankly, that gives us a few more days to try to continue to work on this. So you think you're still trying to get it over the finish line by the time you leave for the August recess, what do you think? You know, that's still my goal. And so I continue to work diligently with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to try to find the sweet spot. But I want to vote on it before we leave for the August recess, because I even personally am losing the ability to muster the enthusiasm after 11 months of negotiating to try to find an answer that pleases everyone. Yeah, it's a great point on the banks talking with the senators and a little fear mongering going on as well. Senator, you've done a great job on this. You've got to feel proud of the leadership and we'll be watching. Thank you so much for walking us through it. Thank you, Maria. All right. Senator Cynthia Lamis joining us. Stay with us. We'll be right back.
